decks.module: Keeping right, yielding and stop lines
decks.domain: Lane travel, speed, pavement markings and space cushion

cards.front: When are you allowed to drive somewhere other than the right side of the road?
cards.back: Keep right except when passing a same-direction vehicle, going left of center around an obstruction, on a one-way road, using the center passing lane of a three-lane road, or when traffic personnel direct you.

cards.front: On a two-way road with no center line, how much room must you leave for oncoming drivers?
cards.back: On a two-way road with no center line, each driver must leave at least half the road to oncoming traffic.

cards.front: What does it mean to yield to another road user?
cards.back: To yield means to slow or stop so another vehicle or a pedestrian can continue safely.
cards.memory_hook: slow or stop, let them go

cards.front: What must you do any time you are driving left of the center line?
cards.back: Whenever you drive left of the center line, for any reason, you must yield to oncoming traffic.

cards.front: Coming out of a driveway, alley or parking lot with no signs or signals, what must you do?
cards.back: Leaving an alley, driveway or parking lot without signs or signals, stop before the road and yield to approaching vehicles and pedestrians.

cards.front: What is the guidance on changing lanes?
cards.back: Change lanes only when safe, and avoid frequent lane changes.

cards.front: If you are driving slower than normal traffic, where should you drive and when should you pull off?
cards.back: If slower than normal traffic, use the right lane or hug the right edge unless preparing to turn left, and pull off at the first safe spot to let a line of traffic pass.
cards.memory_hook: slow stays right, lets lines pass

cards.front: When may a slow driver leave the right lane or right edge?
cards.back: A slow driver keeps to the right lane or right edge, except when getting ready to make a left turn.

cards.front: How is a marked crosswalk shown, and when must you stop at it?
cards.back: A marked crosswalk is shown with white lines, and you must stop when a pedestrian is in it.

cards.front: What is the difference between a stop line and a yield line on the pavement?
cards.back: A stop line is a solid white line across your lane where you must stop, and a yield line is a row of triangles pointing at you where you must yield.

cards.front: What separates a stop line from a yield line?
cards.back: A stop line marks where you must stop, while a yield line of triangles pointing at you marks where you must yield.

decks.domain: Lane travel, speed, pavement markings and space cushion

cards.front: How do Oregon's maximum speed limits relate to the basic rule and to posted signs?
cards.back: Oregon's maximum limits apply on top of the basic rule, mark the top safe speed in ideal conditions, and hold whether or not posted unless another speed is posted.

cards.front: What is the statutory speed limit in alleys and narrow residential areas?
cards.back: The statutory limit is fifteen miles per hour in alleys and narrow residential areas.

cards.front: What is the statutory speed limit in a business district or a school speed zone?
cards.back: The statutory limit is twenty miles per hour in any business district and in a school speed zone.

cards.front: What is the statutory speed limit in residential districts, public parks and ocean shores open to vehicles?
cards.back: The statutory limit is twenty-five miles per hour in residential districts, public parks and on ocean shores where vehicles are allowed.

cards.front: What speed applies on a road that fits no other category, and what about interstates?
cards.back: Roads fitting no other category are fifty-five miles per hour unless posted otherwise, and interstate limits vary.

cards.front: Why do alleys and narrow residential areas have a different limit than ordinary residential districts?
cards.back: Alleys and narrow residential areas carry the lowest statutory limit of fifteen miles per hour, while ordinary residential districts carry twenty-five miles per hour, so the narrowness of the street changes the limit.

cards.front: Which statutory limit does a school speed zone share?
cards.back: A school speed zone shares the twenty miles per hour statutory limit with business districts, not the twenty-five miles per hour limit that applies in residential districts and parks.

cards.front: How does the catch-all statutory limit differ from interstate limits?
cards.back: The fifty-five miles per hour statutory limit covers roads that fit no other category, while interstate highways have limits that vary rather than one fixed statutory figure.

decks.module: Basic rule and variable speed signs
decks.domain: Lane travel, speed, pavement markings and space cushion

cards.front: How do Oregon's digital speed signs decide when to lower the speed?
cards.back: Some Oregon speed signs are digital and use road, weather, traffic and visibility sensors to lower the speed when needed, sometimes showing why.

cards.front: What does a yellow variable advisory speed sign do, and can it be enforced?
cards.back: Yellow variable advisory speed signs recommend a speed and switch on only when needed; they are not limits, but police may enforce them through the basic rule.

cards.front: What does a black-and-white variable speed limit sign do?
cards.back: Black-and-white variable speed limit signs change the actual limit with conditions and are enforced like any speed limit sign.

cards.front: Why do variable speed signs show lower speeds in some conditions?
cards.back: Lower variable speeds add reaction time when fog, rain or snow cut visibility, and add stopping room on sharp curves, steep hills and construction zones.

cards.front: What speed does the basic rule require, and where does it apply?
cards.back: The basic rule requires a speed that is reasonable and cautious for existing conditions, on every road at all times.

cards.front: What must you weigh to obey the basic rule, and does it ever let you exceed the limit?
cards.back: Obeying the basic rule means weighing traffic, pedestrians, cyclists, road surface and width, intersection hazards, weather and visibility; it never permits exceeding the limit.

cards.front: Can you break the basic rule while driving under the posted limit?
cards.back: A speed unsafe for conditions breaks the basic rule even when it is below the posted limit.

cards.front: What counts as racing, and where is it illegal?
cards.back: Racing is illegal on any road and includes any acceleration or speed contest or a speed record attempt.

cards.front: How does a pedestrian's risk of death change as vehicle speed rises?
cards.back: A federal chart shows a pedestrian hit at twenty-three miles per hour has a ten percent risk of death, rising to fifty percent at forty-two miles per hour and ninety percent at fifty-eight miles per hour

cards.front: How does a yellow variable advisory sign differ from a black-and-white variable limit sign?
cards.back: A yellow variable advisory speed sign only recommends a speed, while a black-and-white variable speed limit sign sets an enforceable limit that police treat like any other.
cards.memory_hook: yellow suggests, black and white rules

cards.front: How do the posted limit and the basic rule work together?
cards.back: The posted limit caps your speed in all conditions, while the basic rule can require going slower than that cap; neither one ever allows exceeding the limit.

decks.domain: Lane travel, speed, pavement markings and space cushion

cards.front: What standard do Oregon pavement markings follow, and when may you disregard them?
cards.back: Oregon pavement markings follow national standards and must be obeyed unless a police officer or road worker redirects you.

cards.front: What do yellow lines separate, and what does a solid yellow line mark on a one-way road or ramp?
cards.back: Yellow lines separate opposing traffic and also edge the left side of one-way roads, ramps, shared left-turn lanes and painted medians; a solid yellow line is the left boundary of one-way roads and ramps.

cards.front: What does a broken yellow center line tell drivers on a two-way road?
cards.back: A broken yellow center line marks a two-way road where drivers in both directions may pass.

cards.front: With a solid and a broken yellow line side by side, how do you know whether you may pass?
cards.back: With a solid and a broken yellow line together, you may pass when the broken line is on your side but not when the solid line is.

cards.front: What do double solid yellow lines forbid, and what do they still allow?
cards.back: Double solid yellow lines ban passing both ways, but you may turn left across them into or out of a roadway once oncoming traffic clears.

cards.front: How must you use a two-way left-turn lane?
cards.back: Where a two-way left-turn lane exists, turn left only from it; driving along it is illegal, so enter just before the turn and wait there until clear.

cards.front: What may you do with a painted median edged by double solid yellow lines?
cards.back: A painted median edged by double solid yellow lines may be crossed to turn left after oncoming traffic clears, but it is not a turn lane and may not be driven in.

cards.front: What do yellow diagonal stripes in a painted median mean for drivers?
cards.back: Yellow diagonal stripes in a painted median warn of fixed objects or no-vehicle areas, and driving in or turning across them is illegal.

cards.front: How do broken yellow and double solid yellow center lines differ for passing and turning?
cards.back: A broken yellow center line lets both directions pass, while a double solid yellow line bars passing for both directions but still allows a left turn across it once clear.

cards.front: In a solid-plus-broken yellow pair, which line controls your passing?
cards.back: In a solid-plus-broken yellow pair, only the line nearest your lane counts: broken on your side means you may pass, solid on your side means you may not.

cards.front: How does a two-way left-turn lane differ from a painted median with double yellow lines?
cards.back: A two-way left-turn lane is meant for waiting to turn left, while a painted median with double yellow lines may only be crossed to turn and never used as a turn lane.
cards.memory_hook: wait in one, cross the other

cards.front: What is the basic difference between yellow and white pavement markings?
cards.back: Yellow markings separate traffic going opposite ways, while white markings separate lanes going the same way and mark the right edge.

decks.domain: Lane travel, speed, pavement markings and space cushion

cards.front: What jobs do white pavement markings do on the road?
cards.back: White markings divide same-direction lanes, mark the right edge, and form crosswalks, stop lines, symbols and words; a solid white edge or fog line helps you stay on the road.

cards.front: What does a wide solid white line do, and may you cross it?
cards.back: A wide solid white line channels traffic into lanes such as turn lanes and separates bike lanes; crossing it is allowed but discouraged.

cards.front: What does a broken white line separate, and may you cross it?
cards.back: A broken white line separates same-direction lanes and may be crossed with caution.

cards.front: What does a dotted white line mean before an exit, at a freeway entrance and inside an intersection?
cards.back: A dotted white line may be crossed with caution; before an exit or intersection it means your lane leaves the route, at a freeway entrance it means merge, and in an intersection it guides your lane.

cards.front: What does a double solid white line between lanes mean?
cards.back: A double solid white line means no lane changes and usually comes with a sign banning lane changes for a set distance.

cards.front: How can you recognize a bike lane on the pavement?
cards.back: A bike lane has a wide white line plus a bicycle symbol or bike lane sign and may be painted green.

cards.front: What can white pavement chevrons warn you about?
cards.back: White pavement chevrons may warn of fixed objects ahead or areas closed to vehicles.

cards.front: What do red pavement markings show, and is every transit-only lane red?
cards.back: Red markings show where only transit such as buses, light rail or bikes may travel continuously, but not every transit-only lane is red, so watch signs and markings.

cards.front: What does a solid red lane mean compared with striped red lines?
cards.back: A solid red lane is transit only and may read BUS ONLY, BUS BIKE ONLY or LRT, while striped red lines show where cars may cross in to turn, park or reach a driveway.

cards.front: How do the crossing rules differ among wide solid, broken or dotted, and double solid white lines?
cards.back: A wide solid white line may be crossed but crossing is discouraged, a broken or dotted white line may be crossed with caution, and a double solid white line may not be crossed to change lanes.

cards.front: How does a dotted white line ahead of an exit differ from one at a freeway on-ramp?
cards.back: A dotted white line ahead of an exit means your lane will leave the route, while a dotted white line at a freeway on-ramp means you must merge into freeway traffic.

cards.front: How does a solid red lane differ from striped red lines?
cards.back: A solid red lane is closed to cars, while striped red lines mark the places where a car may enter the transit lane to turn, park or reach a driveway.

decks.domain: Lane travel, speed, pavement markings and space cushion

cards.front: What is a space cushion, and how does speed affect it?
cards.back: A space cushion is room ahead, beside and behind you; the faster you go, the less time you have to spot hazards and react, and the longer it takes to stop.

cards.front: What following distance is safe, and how does it change above thirty miles per hour?
cards.back: A safe following distance is two to four seconds, and above thirty miles per hour it should be four seconds or more.

cards.front: How do you check your following distance while driving?
cards.back: To check your gap, count seconds from when the car ahead passes a fixed mark until you reach it; under two seconds means back off and recount.

cards.front: How far back should you stop behind another vehicle?
cards.back: Stopped behind a vehicle, stay back far enough to see its rear tires meet the road, and rebuild a safe gap once traffic moves.

cards.front: In which situations should you add following distance?
cards.back: Add following distance on wet roads, when someone behind wants to pass, behind bikes or motorcycles, behind large vehicles that cannot see you, when loaded or towing, and in poor visibility.

cards.front: Besides bad weather and big vehicles, when else should you add following distance?
cards.back: Also add following distance when stopped on a hill, where the car ahead may roll back, while learning to drive, and near or in work zones.

cards.front: What affects your stopping distance?
cards.back: Stopping distance depends on road and weather, vehicle weight, reaction time and braking, and it grows with speed even in ideal conditions.

cards.front: How far does it take to stop at sixty miles per hour once you spot a hazard?
cards.back: At sixty miles per hour, the distance from spotting a hazard to a full stop is longer than a football field.

cards.front: How does the general following gap compare with the gap at higher speeds?
cards.back: The general safe following distance is two to four seconds, but at speeds above thirty miles per hour the guidance rises to four seconds or more.
cards.memory_hook: two to four, then four plus

cards.front: How do you add following distance when a driver behind wants to pass?
cards.back: When a driver behind you wants to pass, you add following distance by slowing so there is room in front of you for them to complete the pass.

decks.domain: Lane travel, speed, pavement markings and space cushion

cards.front: How do you keep space beside your vehicle?
cards.back: For side space, avoid riding beside other vehicles on multilane streets, and keep away from oncoming traffic, usually by staying in the center of your lane.

cards.front: How can you help a vehicle entering the freeway or a driver who is signaling?
cards.back: Make room for vehicles entering a freeway by moving over if the lane is clear, and help signaling drivers by easing your speed slightly.

cards.front: Why should you give parked cars extra room?
cards.back: Give parked cars extra room within your lane, since a door may open or a person may step out.

cards.front: How do you keep the driver behind you at a safe distance?
cards.back: Keep the driver behind you back with a steady speed and an early brake tap that lights your brake lights; if tailgated, move right when there is a right lane.

cards.front: What should you do if a tailgater stays behind you and you cannot move over?
cards.back: If a tailgater stays and you cannot move over, slow gradually to invite a pass, and never brake hard to punish tailgating, since you could be rear-ended.

cards.front: What steps keep you safe when backing up?
cards.back: Before backing, look both ways; mirrors miss areas, so turn your head and body right, look out the rear window, glance to each side and back slowly.

cards.front: What is acceptable and what is never acceptable when dealing with a tailgater?
cards.back: With a tailgater behind you, easing off gradually is the advice, while braking hard to scare them off is never acceptable because it risks a rear-end crash.

cards.front: Are mirrors alone enough when you back up?
cards.back: Mirrors alone are not enough for backing; the manual calls for turning your head and body to look out the rear window and glancing to each side.

recaps.module: Keeping right, yielding and stop lines

recap_hooks.text: Stay right unless an exception applies, and yield whenever you cross left of center.
A solid bar across your lane means stop, while a row of triangles means yield.
Alleys are slowest, schools and shops share the next step, and homes and parks come after.
Roads with no other category fall back to the catch-all limit, while interstates vary.

recaps.module: Basic rule and variable speed signs

recap_hooks.text: The basic rule can make a speed under the limit illegal, and it never permits going over.
Yellow variable signs advise, while black-and-white variable signs set the limit.
With paired yellow lines, the line on your side decides whether you may pass.
Wait in a two-way left-turn lane, but only cross a painted median and stay out of diagonal stripes.
Wide solid white is discouraged, broken or dotted white needs caution, and double solid white is off limits.
Solid red is for transit only, and striped red shows where cars may cross in.
Keep two to four seconds of gap, and four or more once you are going faster.
Count from a fixed mark, and back off if you reach it too soon.
Handle a tailgater by moving right or easing off, never by braking hard.
Back up by turning your head and body, not by trusting mirrors alone.
